parties:

vs
Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Finance and others ------ Respondents (in all the writ petitions)
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: In the aforesaid Rules Nisi, the only issue that is raised is as to whether or not the enhancement of the customs duty on the Grey Portland Cement by the Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-1998 by reducing exemption under section 19 of the Customs Act, 1969, hereinafter referred to as the Act, was lawful, valid and constitutional.

2. In the writ petitions, the petitioners are not the same but all of them imported said cement. According to the petitioners, they were entitled to pay duty pursuant to the Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-1998, which exempted duty above 15% and was in force at the time of opening of their letters of credit instead of the duty at the enhanced rate in accordance with the Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-1998 exempting duty above 30% ad valorem under section 19 of the Act.

3. The petitioners imported said cement by opening letters of credit on different dates but

before 20-10-1998 the date when the subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 came into force. The bills of entry for clearance of said cement were also submitted on different dates before and after said date of subsequent Notification.

4. Pursuant to issue of the Rules and directions issued by this Division, the petitioners got release of their respective goods on payment of the duty and other charges on the basis of exemption of duty above 15% in cash and furnishing bank guarantee(s) for the balance between the two rates of exemption.

5. Dr M Zahir, learned Senior Advocate, took us through the relevant provisions of the Act and submitted that the Government acted beyond its jurisdiction in issuing subsequent Notification being SRO dated 20-10-98 enhancing the rate of duty.

6. He submitted that the exemption given by the Notification being SRO No.1 08 dated 11-6-98 and on the basis of which the petitioners opened their letters of credit for import of the cement vested a right in them to get the cement cleared on the basis of earlier rate of exemption that was in force at the time of opening of the letters of credit and the Government was estopped from asking any further duty on the basis of subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-98.

7. In support, he cited the authorities in the Collector of Customs vs A Hannan: 42 DLR (AD) 167; Collector of Customs vs Ahmed Hossain: 48 DLR (AD) 199; Mustafizur Rahman vs Bangladesh: 51 DLR (AD) 40; Commissioner of Customs vs Monohor Ali and others: 2003 BLD (AD) 51 = 8 BLC (AD) 87 = 8 MLR (AD) 113; Bangladesh and others vs Mizanur Rahman: 52 DLR (AD) 149.

8. Mr Nahid Mahtab, learned Deputy Attorney- General for the respondents, first read the subsequent Notification being SRO 233 dated 20-10-98 and submitted that the Government was fully competent to change the rate of exemption under section 19 of the Act and such discretion is now limited to exercise once in a year so as to change the rate of exemption by introduction of the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 19 of the Act by the Act No. 15 of 2000.

9. At our request, Mr Mahmudul Islam, learned Senior Advocate also appeared as an amicus curiae. He took us through the history of development of the concept of vested rights and the principles of estoppel in the matter of levy and collection of customs duty and other charges.

10. He submitted that in view of sections 19,30 and 30A, subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-98 which reduced only the rate of exemption that was earlier granted under section 19 of the Act vide the Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-98 is wholly valid and constitutional and an importer has got no vested right in such exemption.

11. He also read the judgment of A Hannan vs Collector of Customs passed by a Division of this division and reported in 40 DLR 273. He submitted that very basis of the concept of vested rights and/or the principles of estoppel were first initiated in our jurisdiction by a Division Bench presided over Mr Justice Mustafa Kamal, as His Lordship was then, on the view that sections 19 and 30 of the Act were mutually exclusive and independent in their course of operations and in the language of section 19 the Government cannot issue notification with retrospective effect with the canons of construction of delegated legislation. At the time, he submitted, section 30A of the Act was not yet added.

12. We have perused the records of the cases as are available. We have also read the decisions cited. In order to appreciate the submissions of the learned Advocates, we need to read the relevant provisions of the Act, in particular, sections 18, 19, 30 and 30A of the Act, which we would do a little later.

13. Before that, we hope the facts of one case would be sufficient to understand the issue raised and the questions of law involved on the concept of vested rights and/or the principles of estoppel in the matter of levy and collection of the customs duty and other charges pursuant to the provisions of exemption under section 19 of the Act.

14. In Writ Petition No. 3541 of 1998, it is stated that the petitioner on 23-9-98 established a letter of credit for import of 7,000 metric tons of Grey Portland Cement from Indonesia at US$ 41,500 then revised to US$ 2,53,150.00 (15% more or less). At the time, the Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-98 exempting the duty above 15% of said cement ad valorem was in force, Annexure-D to the writ petition. For our understanding, we can say the duty on said cement was 15% only ad valorem at the time, the duty above thereto was exempted. While said cement was on the voyage on the way to Bangladesh, the Government published a Notification being SRO No 233 dated 20-10-98 reducing the exemption from 15% to 30%, thereby enhancing the duty of said cement to 30% ad valorem, Annexure- E. Expecting arrival of the ship at the Chittagong Port by 11-11-98, five bills of entry at the rate of duty at 15% ad valorem were on 5-11-98 submitted. But the customs authority assessed said cement to duty at the rate of 30% on the basis of subsequent Notification being SRO dated 20-10-98 and supplementary duty at the rate of 4% on the basis of the Ordinance No.1 of 1998 for augmenting the rehabilitation of the flood affected people. The petitioner unsuccessfully appealed to respondent No.3, the Commissioner of Customs at Mongla Customs House at Khulna against such assessment. Then, he moved this Division and obtained a Rule nisi and direction for release of the goods at the aforesaid terms.

15. Now, let us read the decisions cited at the Bar. In A Hannan's case, (decided on 9 June, 1998) during the crisis of sugar when the rate of duty was 100%, the Government exempted duty on sugar above 50% by a notification dated 16-10-84. Petitioner opened letter of credit on 31-10-84 for import of 500 metric tons of sugar of South Korean origin and on 24-11-84 the vessel carrying sugar arrived at Chittagong. Meanwhile, the Government by another notification dated 6-11-84 enhanced the rate of duty by exempting duty above 75% ad valorem. Rejection of the customs authority of the prayer of the importer to pay duty at the earlier rate of duty at 50% instead of the new rate of 75% ad valorem was challenged in a writ petition before this Division.

16. A Division Bench of this Division set aside the order on the following views:

"We are absolutely convinced that section 19 of the Customs Act does not provide any "rate of duty" at all. It only provides for exemption of "any goods" from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon. Section 30 does not refer to section 19 at all. To put it plainly. section 30 will operate only insofar as the "rate of duty" levied under section 18 is altered or amended. It has no reference to section 19 at all. To put it plainly, section 30 will operate only insofar as the "rate of duty" levied under section 18 is altered or amended. It has no reference to section 19 at all. Notifications issued under section 19 will follow their own course, independently of section 30, and these notifications will be construed in accordance with the canons of construction of delegated legislation.

.................... .................... .................... ....................

.................... .................... .................... ........................................ ....................

There is nothing in the language of section 19 of the Customs Act to indicate that the Government can issue Notification with retrospective effect."

17. In the appeal therefrom at the instance of the Collector of Customs, the Appellate Division was of the view that,

"That it is a clear case of estoppel, inasmuch as the respondent had acted on the assurance given by the Government and a right vested in him and that could not be taken away. It was no where mentioned in the Notification that the delivery of the bill of entry will be determining factor, as Mr Bhuiyan intends to suggest.

.................... .................... ....................

The respondent acting upon the solemn promise made by the appellant incurred huge expenditures and if the appellant is not held to its promise, the respondent would be put in a disadvantageous position and therefore, the principle of promissory estoppel can also be invoked in this case."

Upon such view, the Appellate Division dismissed the appeal by its decision dated December 6, 1989 reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167.

18. In the case of Ahmed Hossain. 48 DLR (AD) (decided on 9-7-96) forty leave petitions of the Collector of Customs were dismissed. In similar circumstances, the order of this Division setting aside the assessment of duty by the customs authority at the rate of duty as per the Notification issued under section 19 of the Act in force on the date of bill of entry presented and not the Notification in force on the date of opening of the letter of credit for import of Red Cow Condensed Milk was upheld. The Appellate Division considered and approved the case of A. Hannan on the following view:

"We do not think that the difference in facts would make any difference in the application of the principle which is based on interpretation of sections 19 and 30 of the Customs Act, 1969."

19. Insertion of section 30A of the Act was noticed by the Appellate Division for the first time and disposed of the submissions on the change in law with the following view:

"It will be merely academic now to try and resolve the alleged conflict of decisions with regard to the interpretation of sections 19 and 30 as argued by the learned Additional Attorney- General."

20. In the case of Mizanur Rahman, 52 DLR (AD) 149 (decided on 1-6-2000), the Appellate Division set aside the decision of this Division and allowed the appeal accepting the assessment on the enhanced rate of tariff value on the imported G. Plain Sheets that was in force on the date of bill of entry presented and not on the rate of tariff value on the date of opening of letter of credit on the following views:

"The argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in a special circumstance as in Hannan s case but it is difficult to understand the normal importer would acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of letter of credit.

.................... .................... ...................

The customs duty payable on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of the bill of entry and not on the basis of invoice value or tariff in force at the time of opening of the letter of credit.

.................... .................... ....................

No vested right is acquired by the importer to pay sales tax and customs duty on the basis of tariff value declared by notification in force on the date of opening the letter of credit. The importer has to pay tax and duty on the basis of tariff value in force on the date of presentation of bill of entry."

It also held that

"So, the decision in 51 DLR (AD) 40 (Mustafizur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and 6 others) appears to us not correctly decided due to the failure of the then Attorney-General to point out the distinction between 42 DLR (AD) 167 and 48 DLR (AD) 199 on the one hand and the case of Mustafizur Rahman on the other."

21. In Monohar Ali, (2003 23 BLD (AD) 59 = 8 MLR (AD) 113 (decided on 13-7-2002) the withdrawal of CRF scheme before the presentation of the bill of entry for clearance of imported goods came up for consideration. Section 30A was considered of course, vis-a-vis section 25A of the Act. In allowing the appeal, the Appellate Division held-

" ........... section 30A came into effect on 1-7-95 and the present consignments were imported subsequent to that date. However, it also appears that both section 30A and section 25A came into operation on the same date i.e. on 1-7-95 but in section 30A there is nothing to suggest that it excluded the operation of section 25A of the Customs Act.

.................... .................... ....................

at the relevant time the section contained non-obstante clause like, "Notwithstanding anything contained in any other section of this Act; which means that it included 30A of the Customs Act.

Therefore, section 25A would prevail over all other sections including sections 25(7) and section 30A of the Customs Act."

(underlined by us)

22. The ratio decidendi of the decision as under- lined by us appears to be that because of the non-obstante clause, section 25A providing the CRF value of the imported goods would prevail over all other provisions of the Act including sub-section (7) of section 25 (levy of tariff value) and section 30A (value and effective rate of duty) of the Customs Act. In holding such view, it relied upon a number of decisions including that of A Hannan.

23. In the case of Selim (Haji) vs Collector of Customs: 54 DLR 287, a Division Bench of this division considered for the first time the scope of the exemption under section 19 in the context of section 30 and 30A. It discharged the Rule on the following views:

" ... that once exemption is granted as to imposition of customs duty the same cannot be changed or varied does not have any leg to stand and for that reason the said proviso has been added later on with the provision of section 19(1) and in this case, we have already stated that the bill of entries were submitted before the proviso came in and therefore, it is not applicable.

We have already stated that it is neither increasing or decreasing. It can be called a with drawal of the exemption. So, it is very much within the jurisdiction of the customs authority to withdraw the exemption, as was before the addition of the said proviso, up to the ceiling as affixed by the 1st Schedule of the Finance Act. So, the argument of Dr Zahir, having no substance in this respect, it is repelled."

24. We have closely read the aforesaid decisions particularly those of the Appellate Division. We find in the case of A. Hannan only the scope of section 19 of the Act empowering exemption was considered. It is also noted that after said decision, section 30A was inserted in the Act with effect from July 1, 1995. After such insertion, section 30A was just noticed in the case of Ahmed Hossain disposing 40 leave petitions but no interpretation or construction of section 30A in the context of sections 19 and 30 was thought to be necessary since the case was not on the exemption under section 19 of the Act. In the case of Monohar Ali, section 30A was for the first time considered by the Appellate Division and in the context of section 25(7) and section 30 of the Act. In the case of Mizanur Rahman, the Appellate Division in dispelling the argument on the concept of vested rights and principles of estoppel regarding levy of tariff value under section 25(7) observed: "The argument of acquiring vested right may be tenable in case of exemption granted in a special circumstance as in Hannan s case but it is difficult to understand the normal importer would acquire vested right in the invoice value or the tariff value prevailing at the time of opening of letter of credit". So, the decision of the High Court Division in the case of A. Hannan on exemption under section 19 of the Act before the insertion of section 30A in the Act upheld by the Appellate Division was referred to the cases of Ahmed Hossain, Mizanur Rahman and Monohar Ali on different contexts.

25. Now, we shall examine the relevant provisions of the Act with regard to exemption of the duty, in particular sections 18, 19,30 and 30A of the Act, which were at the relevant time as follows:

18. Goods Dutiable: (1) Except as hereinafter provided, customs duties shall be levied at such rates as are prescribed in the First Schedule or under any other law for the time being in force on-

(a) goods imported into, or exported from, Bangladesh ;

(b) goods brought from any foreign country to any customs station, and without payment of duty there, transshipped or transported for, or thence carried to, and imported at, any other customs station; and

(c) goods brought in bond from one customs-station to another.

(2) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, levy, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions as it may deem fit to impose, a regulatory duty on all or any of the goods specified in the First Schedule at a rate not exceeding fifty percent of the rate, if any specified therein read with any notification issued under sub-section (1) of section 2 or sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Protective Duties Act. 1950 (LXI of 1950) Or at a rate not exceeding hundred percent of the value of such goods as determined under section 25.

(3) The regulatory duty levied under sub- section (2) shall be in addition to any duty imposed under sub-section (1) or under any other law for the time being in force.

(4) Any notification issued under sub-section (2) shall, if not earlier rescinded, stand rescinded on the expiry of the financial year in which it was issued]

19. General power to exempt from customs-duties. If the Government is satisfied, after consultation with the Board, that it is necessary in the public interest to do so, it may, subject to such conditions, limitations or restrictions, if any, as it thinks fit to impose, by notification in the official Gazette, exempt any goods imported into, or exported from Bangladesh or into or from any specified port or station or area therein, from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon.

(2) An exemption granted under sub- section (1) shall be effective from the date mentioned in the notification issued under that sub- section.

30. Date for determination of rate of duty and tariff value of imported goods. The rate of duty and tariff value, if any, applicable to any imported goods, shall be the rate of duty and tariff value in force,

a) in the case of goods cleared for home consumption section 79, on the date a bill of entry is presented under section and a bill of entry number is allocated thereto;

(b) in the case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption under section 104, on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the warehouse, and

(c) in the case of any other goods, on the date of payment of duty.

Provided that if a bill of entry is presented in anticipation of arrival of a conveyance by which the goods are imported, the relevant date for .the purpose of this section shall be the date on which the manifest of the conveyance is delivered after its arrival.

31A. Value and effective rate of duty- Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force or any decision of any court, for the purposes of section 30, the value and the rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed under section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duty, that may have become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for the sale of such goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof.

26. Close reading of the above provisions on exemption make it clear to us that the customs-duty shall be levied at such rates as are prescribed in the First Schedule or under any other law for the time being in force on goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh. First Schedule is always passed by the Parliament along with the Finance Act under section 18 of the Act. Such levy of duty by the Parliament does not appear to be absolute in view of the qualifying clause at the beginning of the section that "Except as hereinafter provided" that subject to other provisions of the Act. Section 19 of the Act, on the other hand, empowers the Government to exempt any goods imported into or exported from Bangladesh by notification in the official gazette from the whole or any part of the customs-duties chargeable thereon, obviously under section 18. Before declaring such exemption, the Government, of course, shall consult with the National Board of Revenue and be satisfied that such exemption was necessary in the public interest.

27. The following proviso was subsequently inserted in sub-section (1) of section 19 of the Act,

Provided that if, in a financial year, exemption under this sub-section is given in respect of any goods the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year so as to increase that rate.

28. Any exemption under section 19 of the Act shall naturally affect the rate( s) of duty levied by the Parliament in the First Schedule or otherwise to change. Such power of the Government to exempt duty is clearly intended by the Parliament to affect the rate(s) of duty levied by it. After insertion of the proviso to sub-section (1), the Parliament clearly ordained that in a financial year the rate of duty cannot be changed more than once in that year in which year if any exemption is given to increase that rate. Plain meaning of such proviso appears to us that the Government cannot exercise its power to declare exemption more than once in a financial year to increase the rate of duty in that very year. Mr. Mahmudul Islam told us that during the crisis of sugar in the country in 1980s exemption of the customs duty was declared many a times in a year causing some kind of unrest in the market of sugar. So, the Parliament had to intervene and insert the proviso limiting the time of exercise of the Government power.

29. Section 30 of the Act clearly provides that the rate of duty and tariff value shall be the rate of duty and tariff value in force on the date the bill of entry is presented under section 79 in case of goods cleared and under section 104 in case of goods cleared from a warehouse for home consumption. Such rate of duty must be the rate which suffered change after any exemption declared by the Government under section 19 of the Act. Introduction of section 30A in the Act, we believe, removed all controversies or confusion created, particularly by the decisions in the case of A. Hannan relating to the effective rate of duty and date of enforcement of such rate.

<u>30. In view of the opening non obstante clause in section 30A, "Notwithstanding any decision of any Court, for the purpose of section 30," the value and rate of duty applicable to any goods shall respectively include the value as determined under section 25 and any amount of duty imposed by section 18, 18A or 18B and the amount of duty that may become payable in consequence of the withdrawal of the whole or any part of the exemption or concession from duty say under section 19 whether before or after the conclusion of a contract or agreement for sale of goods or opening of a letter of credit in respect thereof. Under the sweep of such obstante clause, the binding effect of the authority of A Hannan decided on 9-7-89 on the doctrine of vested rights and/or the principles of estoppel in the matter of exemption of customs duty deems to have been washed away. After introduction of section 30A, the rate(s) of duty on any goods levied under section 18 if was affected to change by any Notification issued by the Government exempting the whole or any part of the rate(s) of duty on such goods under section 19 such changed rate(s) of duty would be in force on the date of presentation of a bill of entry for clearance of goods under section 30 of the Act without any reference to the date of opening of a letter of credit.</u>

<u>31. For the reasons aforesaid, there is no substance in the submissions of Dr Zahir. We find subsequent Notification being SRO No. 233 dated 20-10-98 valid, competent and constitutional and the importers had no vested rights in the rate of exemption first declared by earlier Notification being SRO No. 108 dated 11-6-98, which was changed by subsequent Notification increasing the rate of duty.</u>

32. In the result, all the above Rules are discharged with cost.

The Customs Authority shall be at liberty to encash the bank guarantees if the petitioners do not pay in cash the amount of money covered by respective bank guarantees within a period of thirty days of receipt of this order.

End.
